summary:
Jeju Special Self-Governing Province stands under the national framework of South Korea. Civilian law does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception sits in the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, a provision the Constitutional Court upheld in 2023. Enforcement has been punitive and targeted, including a 2017 military investigation that Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt and that led to criminal charges against 32 personnel, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The sharpest documented harm to a trans person in the national framework concerns Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel treated the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available on Jeju and the surgical prerequisite has fallen away. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that conditioning gender change on surgery is contrary to law and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now reference rather than criteria. The court stated that every person has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity. The ruling removed the surgical prerequisite nationwide, including on Jeju, where the reporting identifies no specific case. The Supreme Court ruled en banc on 24 November 2022 that transgender people with minor children can obtain legal gender recognition provided they are unmarried, overturning an 11-year-old precedent; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required applicants to be over 20, single and childless.

Restroom access is a documented legal and practical issue. On 22 July 2024 the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, holding that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, whose family-register gender change had been approved in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights, and that comfortable use of restrooms is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found 41% avoided facilities out of fear. These national rulings govern Jeju, and the reporting records no specific incident on the island.

School environments show the same pattern. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms to avoid being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding in and leaving school early, and researchers called for legal and institutional reform to make school environments safer.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare refused a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence concentrates at public events. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when roughly 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, after which organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people and doxing and online harassment rose. Surveys record the wider burden: 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates in a 2014 finding, 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma, and a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the previous year.

South Korean law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, although a 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area and LGBTI organisations can register, an NGO having won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 amid what Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction. A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care, and Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people alongside an otherwise relatively positive record on free media and civil society.
tangentialFactors:
Hostility in the national framework surfaces most visibly at Pride events and in schools rather than in routine street crime, so an openly trans visitor on Jeju faces lower exposure than at mainland gatherings where anti-LGBT protests have turned violent. The island's own sources report no Pride-related assault or protest incident.

The 2024 restroom ruling and the 2021 National Human Rights Commission survey concern state conduct and facility access generally, not Jeju-specific practice; the same applies to the DDing Dong school research, which draws on mainland school settings.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 assesses free media and civil society as relatively positive overall, which affects how readily a visitor can seek help or report mistreatment locally.

South Korea's position sits in contrast to jurisdictions that criminalise consensual same-sex conduct in civilian life, and in contrast to states that require surgery for legal gender recognition; the surgical condition fell on 8 May 2024 and the civilian criminalisation gap does not apply here.

General street crime, transport safety and standard entry logistics for Jeju are outside this record and are not assessed from the sources supplied.
localsOnly:
Residents of Jeju change registered sex through the family-register court process, and since the 8 May 2024 Yeongdong ruling no sex-reassignment surgery is required; court guidelines that once demanded surgery operate as reference rather than criteria.

Transgender residents are excluded from military service, while consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel remains criminal under article 92-6 with a sentence of up to two years, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023.

Transgender parents who are unmarried can obtain legal gender recognition following the Supreme Court's en banc ruling of 24 November 2022, which reversed an 11-year-old precedent; the earlier 2011 requirement that applicants be over 20, single and without children no longer stands.

Residents have no comprehensive statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, since no national anti-discrimination law has been enacted, and same-sex couples cannot marry or jointly adopt.

Same-sex partners gained a defined healthcare entitlement through the 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on partner healthcare rights, while hospitalisation itself remains without dedicated guidelines after the Ministry of Health and Welfare declined to draft them in 2023.

National Human Rights Commission findings and the appellate restroom judgment bind the state on Jeju as elsewhere, so police advice that restricts a trans person's use of public facilities is actionable.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Jeju-specific incident involving a trans visitor, and no Jeju-specific enforcement record, is available in the sources; the island's position is derived from national rulings and no local case is documented either way.

Whether Jeju Special Self-Governing Province has enacted its own provincial human rights or anti-discrimination ordinance, and what protection that would offer, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

Trans competence of healthcare providers on Jeju, and the practical availability of transition-related care on the island, are not covered by the inventory.

Detention, prison or immigration-holding conditions for a trans person on Jeju, and how gender is placed in identity documents at the island's ports of entry, are not sourced.

Whether the 41% facility-avoidance figure from the 2021 National Human Rights Commission survey includes Jeju respondents is not stated.
